title: Assignment, Comparison, and Short-Circuit Evaluation

options.text: The program prints `2 5`.
The expression `(x = 2)` evaluates as true.
The assignment `(y = x + 3)` is skipped because of short-circuit evaluation.
After the condition is evaluated, `x` is 2 and `y` is 5.
Replacing `(x = 2)` with `(x = 0)` would prevent `(y = x + 3)` from being evaluated.

explanation: `x = 2` assigns 2 to `x` and evaluates to the nonzero value 2, which is true. Therefore the right side of `&&` is evaluated. `y = x + 3` assigns 5 to `y`, which is also true. The body executes and prints `2 5`. If the first assignment instead produced 0, `&&` would short-circuit and the assignment to `y` would not execute.

title: Finding the Boundary Errors in an Else-If Chain

options.text: A score of 90 incorrectly produces `F`.
A score of 80 incorrectly produces `F`.
A score of 70 produces `C`.
A score of 100 produces `A`.
Changing the first two lower-bound comparisons from `>` to `>=` is sufficient to fix the intended 90 and 80 boundary cases.

explanation: At 90, the first condition fails because it requires `score > 90`, while the second fails because it requires `score < 90`; therefore 90 reaches `F`. Similarly, 80 fails the second condition because it requires `score > 80` and fails the third because it requires `score < 80`. Scores 70 and 100 are handled correctly. Using `score >= 90` and `score >= 80` fixes those two intended boundary gaps.

title: Switch Fall-Through and Entry Point

options.text: With `n = 2`, the output is `BC`.
With `n = 1`, the output is `ABC`.
With `n = 3`, the output is `C`.
With `n = 4`, the output is `DE`.
With `n = 5`, nothing is printed because no numbered case matches.

explanation: A matching case determines where execution begins, but execution continues until a `break` or the end of the switch. Thus 2 produces `BC`, 1 produces `ABC`, 3 produces `C`, and 4 falls through into `default`, producing `DE`. If `n = 5`, `default` executes and prints `E`.

title: Nested If and Dangling Else Analysis

options.text: For the given values, the program prints `B`.
The first `else` is associated with `if (y > 5)`.
If `x` were 2, the program would print `C` regardless of the value of `y`.
If `x` were 8 and `y` were 10, the program would print `A`.
The indentation forces the first `else` to belong to `if (x > 5)`.

explanation: Without braces, an `else` is associated with the nearest unmatched `if`. Therefore the first `else` belongs to `if (y > 5)`. For `x=8, y=3`, the output is `B`. If the outer condition is false, the outer `else` prints `C`. Indentation has no effect on the grammatical association.

title: Chained Comparisons That Look Correct

options.text: The program prints `Inside`.
The condition is parsed as `(0 < x) < 10`.
The result of `0 < x` can participate in the second comparison as a value equivalent to 0 or 1.
The correct conventional test for the intended range is `0 < x && x < 10`.
C++ rejects the original condition as a syntax error.

explanation: Relational operators associate left-to-right, so the expression is parsed as `(0 < x) < 10`. With `x=50`, `0 < 50` is true. In the comparison with 10, that Boolean value is converted to 1, making `1 < 10` true. The intended range test should use two comparisons joined by `&&`.

title: Short-Circuit Operators and Hidden Side Effects

options.text: The first `++y` is not evaluated.
The second `++y` is not evaluated.
The final value of `y` is 5.
The program prints `5`.
The first `if` prints `A` because `++y > 5` would be true.

explanation: In the first condition, `x != 0` is false, so `&&` short-circuits and `++y` is skipped. In the second condition, `x == 0` is true, so `||` short-circuits and its `++y` is also skipped. Therefore `y` remains 5, the first body does not execute, and the second body prints `5`.

title: Debugging an Invalid Switch Statement

options.text: Change `choice` to a `double` and use it directly as the switch condition.
Add another `case 2:` label to the same switch.
Remove both `break` statements.
Move the `default` label before `case 1:`.
Replace `case 2:` with `case 1 + 1:` while keeping `case 1:`.

explanation: A `double` cannot be used directly as the controlling expression of a standard C++ switch, and duplicate case values are not allowed. Removing `break` statements is legal but introduces fall-through. `default` may appear anywhere inside the switch. Replacing `case 2` with `case 1 + 1` is also valid because `1 + 1` is an integral constant expression equal to 2 and does not duplicate `case 1`.

title: Ternary Operator, Type Conversion, and Integer Arithmetic

options.text: The condition `a < b` is false.
The selected expression is `a / b`.
The arithmetic operation in the selected branch produces the integer value 2 before the result is converted.
`result` ultimately contains `2.0`.
`result` contains `2.25` because its declared type is `double`.

explanation: `9 < 4` is false, so the expression associated with the false branch, `a / b`, determines the value. Since both operands of that division are integers, `9 / 4` evaluates to 2. The conditional expression's common type is affected by the other `double` branch, so the selected value is converted to `double`, and `result` becomes `2.0`, not `2.25`.

title: Nested Ternary Operator Decision Path

options.text: The first condition `x > y` is false.
The expression is interpreted as `x > y ? 10 : (y > z ? 20 : (x == z ? 30 : 40))`.
`result` becomes 20.
The condition `x == z` must be evaluated before `result` can be determined.
Changing `y` from 6 to 2 while leaving `x=6` and `z=3` would make `result` equal 10.

explanation: The conditional operator is right-associative. With `x=6` and `y=6`, `x > y` is false, so evaluation proceeds to `y > z`. Since `6 > 3` is true, 20 is selected and `x == z` is not evaluated. If `y` were changed to 2, the first condition `6 > 2` would be true and the result would instead be 10.

title: Multiple Independent If Statements Versus Else-If

options.text: The program prints `ABD`.
The `else` is associated only with `if (x > 20)`.
Both of the first two `if` bodies execute.
Changing the second and third `if` keywords to `else if` would change the output for `x = 15`.
The program prints only `A` because once one `if` succeeds, all later conditions are skipped.

explanation: These are three independent `if` statements, except that the final `else` belongs specifically to the third `if`. Since `15 > 5` and `15 > 10` are true, `A` and `B` are printed. Since `15 > 20` is false, its `else` prints `D`, giving `ABD`. If the latter conditions were changed to `else if`, the first successful branch would prevent the later branches from being evaluated, so the output would change.
